cells.tense: You are giving and taking in equal measure while the ground stays bare.
cells.act: set the finished thing down in a form that keeps
cells.ask: Take a practice the ending left you and put it somewhere it stays put — a day, a shelf, a line you wrote. Leave it alone, and let it hold itself.
cells.core:
What's ended has left a clearing, and the exchange between you and other people is even here. You give what you have and you take what's offered, and nobody is carrying more than their share of the work. That evenness is the harvest of the ending, not a break from it — you cleared the ground so something fair could stand on it. The give and take is what keeps the clearing from closing over.

You've already balanced a lot by hand to keep it that way. The next piece is holding the form. Take one practice or arrangement the ending produced and set it somewhere steady — a place, a day, a written line — so it holds whether or not you're paying attention. Then the clearance stays open even on the days you're tired. Nothing has to be added to it. The hold is the work.
cells.sheetLine: The clearing is fair ground, and you're keeping it open.
cells.verb: giving and receiving in equal measure
cells.place: a clearing left after something ends

cells.tense: You will be counted on for a fairness that hasn't happened yet, and you are already braced.
cells.act: carry your own share, all of it
cells.ask: Pick a day and run it on your own fuel — no tallying who gave what, no watching to see who shows. Do your share, then let the day close.
cells.core:
You're bracing for an ending that hasn't arrived, holding a fairness nobody has tested yet. The ledger is open in your head before anyone has taken anything, and the counting runs the clearing instead of the clearing running it. You give with one hand and watch with the other, and whoever is standing in the clearing with you can sense the scale they're being weighed on.

Fairness this tight stops the exchange it was protecting. For one day, meet what's around you from your own supply and count nothing — not favors given, not favors owed, not whether the share came out even. Let the day close without a verdict. If something is genuinely off, it will still be off tomorrow and simpler to see then. The pressure you're carrying lifts when you stop checking it every mile.
cells.sheetLine: The tally is running before anything has happened.

cells.tense: You have been giving to something that already closed, and the return has thinned.
cells.act: strike one thing from the list that does not serve
cells.ask: The next time you feel the pull to give where the ending already finished, notice it and let it pass through you without acting. Then see what's left.
cells.core:
Something ended, and you're still giving to it. The clearing is here, but you keep reaching into the empty ground — old obligations, old arrangements, old fairness — and what comes back to you is thinner each time. Receiving has gotten harder than giving, or you've stopped expecting the return at all. The closed doorway isn't in the road ahead anymore, and you're still turned toward it.

Look closer at what you're actually holding. Some of what you tend is finished, and some is alive, and close attention will tell you which is which — the finished ones feel like obligation, the living ones feel like weight you chose. Let the finished ones drop, one at a time, as they come. Then let something come back: an hour, a rest, a small return from the clearing. Telling the two apart is the skill, and you have it.
cells.sheetLine: You're giving to a door that already closed.
cells.verb: giving and receiving in equal measure
cells.place: a clearing left after something ends

cells.tense: You are attending to what ended and what comes next, not naming your own hand in it.
cells.act: hold two true things without declaring either
cells.ask: Next time you even something up, let yourself know who's doing it, hold that a beat without judging it, and leave it there.
cells.core:
In this clearing, the fairness gets done by someone, and that someone is you. You notice who's short, you quietly make it right, you step back so the share comes out even. Asked about it, you'd say the situation sorted itself. The balancing is something your hands do that you don't file under your own name. The endings here look like things that happened to you rather than choices you made inside them.

Hold that longer before you label it. Just before you even something up, let yourself know the act is yours — and sit with it without deciding whether that's generous, controlling, or nothing much. Both can be true at once. A bystander and a person actually here differ only in that the second one knows what they did. Keep knowing it for a moment, then let the moment pass.
